sourceReview: See CLASS6-ENGLISH1-SOURCE-REVIEW.md. Seen passages manually transcribed from cited pages; minor punctuation/line-break normalisation only.

passages.text:
Bulbul collects rubbish from the Sankar area in Dhaka. Every morning, he wakes up at 5 o'clock and walks along the streets of Sankar to collect rubbish. People of Sankar put their rubbish in plastic bins and leave them in front of their houses. Bulbul walks from door to door to collect them. Sometimes the bins are very dirty and they smell bad. But Bulbul does not mind. He takes out everything from the bins and puts them in his van. He believes that all jobs are important. He works hard every day to keep his area clean.

Last month Bulbul was sick for two days. So, he could not come to collect the rubbish. The people of Sankar were in great trouble. They got piles of rubbish waiting in front of their houses. The whole area became dirty and unhygienic. When Bulbul got well, he came back to Sankar. He collected everything from all the bins. Bulbul does not want to fall sick again. He realises, if he stops working even for a few days only, the whole area will turn into a big dustbin.

A proverb says 'Health is Wealth'. To keep healthy is to keep free from disease and anxiety. Good health is proper functioning of all body organs. It is also feeling well both in body and in mind. People in good health are active, cheerful and happy. If you are healthy, you can be happy and can help others in society as well.

To keep in good health we should be careful about hygiene. The rules and practices of keeping good health are called hygiene. We must practise the rules of hygiene. Proper food and nutrition, physical exercise, rest and sleep, cleanliness, and proper medicare are essential for good health.

On Thursday, thirty pupils from Riverbank School visited a small local museum. Before leaving, their teacher, Mr Sen, divided them into five groups. Each group received a different question to investigate. His purpose was to help everyone look closely instead of simply copying labels.

At the entrance, a guide explained two rules: visitors must not touch the objects, and they should speak quietly. Sami was interested in an old wooden boat. He first thought it was a toy, but the label said that fishers had used it on a nearby river. The guide explained that the river had once been an important route for travel and trade.

In another room, the pupils saw a display of woven baskets. There was no date on one label. Rather than guessing, Liza wrote, "Date not given," in her notebook and prepared a question for the guide. The guide promised to check the museum records; she did not provide a date immediately.

Back at school, each group presented one finding and one unanswered question. The class learned that a good visitor notices details, respects shared objects and admits when information is missing.
passages.note: Originally authored for practice pack 002. Teacher must replace if previously taught to these pupils; unseen is relative to learner exposure.

questions.instruction: Read S1 and choose the best answer. (1 × 7 = 7)

items.question: Where does Bulbul collect rubbish?
items.explanation: Section B identifies the locality and city.

items.question: When does Bulbul wake up each morning?
Where do residents leave their rubbish for collection?

options.C: In plastic bins in front of their houses
options.D: On the roofs of their homes

items.explanation: The collection arrangement is described in Section B.

items.question: What does Bulbul use to carry the collected rubbish?
items.explanation: He empties the bins and puts their contents in his van.

items.question: Why did Bulbul miss two days of work last month?
items.explanation: The reason for absence is illness, not unwillingness to work.

items.question: What happened while Bulbul could not collect rubbish?

options.D: The area became dirty and unhygienic

items.explanation: Piles accumulated outside houses during his absence.

items.question: What belief about work does Bulbul express?

options.D: Every job has the same timetable

items.explanation: This belief is explicit; it does not mean all jobs have identical tasks.

questions.instruction: Answer the five questions from S1. (2 × 5 = 10)

items.question: How does Bulbul collect rubbish from the houses?
items.modelAnswer: He goes from door to door, takes the rubbish from the bins and puts it in his van.

items.question: What did Bulbul do after recovering from illness?
items.modelAnswer: He returned to Sankar and collected everything from the bins.

items.question: How does his absence show the value of his work?
items.modelAnswer: When he was absent, rubbish piled up and the area became unhygienic. This shows that his regular work helps keep the neighbourhood clean.

items.question: According to Bulbul, what might happen if his work stopped for a few days?
items.modelAnswer: He believes the whole area would turn into a large dump because rubbish would remain uncollected.

items.question: What respectful thing could you say to Bulbul?
items.modelAnswer: I could say, “Thank you for helping to keep our neighbourhood clean. Your work is important.”

questions.instruction: Complete the following passage with suitable words from S2. Use one word in each gap. (1 × 5 = 5)
questions.text: The passage connects good health with both body and (a) ____. It says people in good health are active, (b) ____ and happy. Health-maintaining rules and practices are called (c) ____. Proper food and (d) ____, exercise, rest and (e) ____ are among the essentials mentioned.

questions.instruction: Write a summary of U1 in your own words. (10)
questions.modelAnswer: Pupils visited a local museum in groups to investigate different questions. They followed the museum rules and used labels and a guide to understand the objects. When information was missing, they recorded a question instead of guessing. Their reports showed the value of careful observation, respect and honest inquiry.
assessment: Captures the main situation and outcome
Selects key ideas rather than minor details

questions.instruction: Match the parts in columns A and B to make five complete sentences. Use each ending once. (1 × 5 = 5)

endings.A: Liza recorded that it was not given.
endings.B: each group shared a finding and a question.
endings.E: visitors were told not to touch them.

questions.instruction: Put the eight sentences in the correct order. Write only the corresponding letters. (1 × 8 = 8)

sentences.A: With the timetable checked, she chose a suitable morning service.
sentences.B: After choosing the service, she asked her father to book the tickets.
sentences.C: The following morning, the family reached the station with those tickets.
sentences.D: First, Nila checked the train timetable for her family trip.
sentences.E: Once seated on the train, they put their bags safely beside them.
sentences.F: When their train arrived, they boarded it and found their seats.
sentences.G: After settling their bags, they watched the train leave the platform.
sentences.H: Before boarding, they waited behind the marked safety line.

questions.explanation: The sequence follows checking, choosing, booking, reaching, waiting, boarding, storing and departing. The reference to seats before settling bags fixes the last steps.

questions.instruction: Answer any five of the eight questions from the textbook poems. The full poems are not reproduced. (2 × 5 = 10)

items.question: How are the elephants described as holding hands?
items.modelAnswer: They are described as holding hands by holding one another’s tails.

items.question: What does the poem suggest about trunks and tails?
items.modelAnswer: It calls them handy things, showing that they are useful for keeping the elephants linked while walking.

items.question: What does the bow that bridges heaven refer to?
items.modelAnswer: It refers to a rainbow arching across the sky.

items.question: What is a reasonable main idea of the poem?
items.modelAnswer: The poem celebrates natural beauty by presenting clouds and the rainbow as even prettier than boats, ships and river bridges.

items.question: What difficulty with English does the poem illustrate?
items.modelAnswer: It illustrates that similar spellings can have different pronunciations and that spelling alone does not reliably predict every sound.

items.question: What tone does the poem create? Give a reason.
items.modelAnswer: It creates a playful, humorous tone by presenting a crowded series of tricky words and joking about the speaker’s struggles.

items.question: Whom does the speaker finally choose?
items.modelAnswer: The speaker chooses the same parents they have always had.

items.question: What is one supported theme of the poem?
items.modelAnswer: The poem expresses the speaker’s affection and appreciation for their own parents through the imagined choice in a dream.

questions.instruction: Read the opening and complete the story in at least ten new sentences. Give a suitable title. (10)
questions.opening: One afternoon, Rafi was leaving school when he noticed a small bag near the gate. He looked around, but nobody seemed to be looking for it. He decided to ask an adult for help.
questions.modelTitle: The Bag at the School Gate
questions.modelAnswer: Rafi stopped beside the bag. He did not know who owned it. He called the teacher who was standing near the gate. Together, they took the bag to the school office. The teacher checked for a name while Rafi waited. A label inside named a pupil from another class. The office contacted that pupil’s class teacher. Soon a worried child arrived and described the bag. The teachers checked that it was really hers before returning it. She thanked Rafi for reporting what he had found. Rafi felt pleased that he had asked for help instead of guessing.
assessment: At least ten new sentences and a suitable title

questions.instruction: Write a paragraph on “Your First Day at School” in 120 words. (10)
questions.modelAnswer: My first day at my new school began with mixed feelings. I felt excited about meeting classmates, but I was also a little nervous. My mother took me to the school gate and wished me well. Inside, a teacher showed me the way to my classroom. A pupil smiled and offered me a seat beside her. During the break, she introduced me to two friends. They explained where we kept our books and how to borrow a library book. I asked questions whenever I was unsure. By the end of the day, the building no longer felt strange. I went home feeling welcome and hopeful. That day taught me how small acts of kindness can help a newcomer feel comfortable.
assessment: Relevant first-person account with reasons for feelings
Appropriate punctuation and the requested length
questions.note: Original first-person example, not Tarun’s biography.

questions.instruction: Write a dialogue between a pupil and a museum guide about an object whose label has incomplete information. (10)

modelAnswer.speaker: Pupil
modelAnswer.line: Excuse me, may I ask about this basket?

modelAnswer.speaker: Guide
modelAnswer.line: Of course. What would you like to know?

modelAnswer.speaker: Pupil
modelAnswer.line: The label describes its use, but I cannot find a date. When was it made?

modelAnswer.speaker: Guide
modelAnswer.line: I do not have a confirmed date at the moment.

modelAnswer.speaker: Pupil
modelAnswer.line: Should I write an approximate year in my notebook?

modelAnswer.speaker: Guide
modelAnswer.line: Please write that the date is not given. We should not guess.

modelAnswer.speaker: Pupil
modelAnswer.line: Is there another source we could check?

modelAnswer.speaker: Guide
modelAnswer.line: I can check the museum records and ask the curator.

modelAnswer.speaker: Pupil
modelAnswer.line: Thank you. I will keep the question in my notes.

modelAnswer.speaker: Guide
modelAnswer.line: You are welcome. Asking careful questions is part of learning.

assessment: Has a relevant exchange of questions and responses
questions.note: Original model response. Other relevant, coherent answers are acceptable; no official marks or word limit assigned.

1.rule: One mark per correct option; no negative marking in this draft.

2.rule: Two marks each: 2 for a complete accurate answer, 1 for a relevant partial answer, 0 for an incorrect/absent answer. Accept equivalent wording and supported inference/opinion where the prompt allows it.

3.rule: One mark per suitable word. Accept a defensible equivalent if grammar and passage meaning remain accurate.

4.rule: One mark per appropriate contextual synonym/antonym, including accurate alternatives not listed.

5.rule: One mark per correct information cell; accept numerals or words.

6.rule: For a true statement, 1 for True; for a false statement, 0.5 for False and 0.5 for an accurate correction. This split is author-proposed, not asserted as an official instruction.

8.rule: One mark for each correctly matched complete sentence.

9.rule: One mark for each letter in its correct position. This partial-credit method is author-proposed.

10.rule: Mark the first five responses submitted: each receives 1 for an accurate relevant idea and 1 for supporting explanation/detail. Teacher must announce any different excess-answer policy before use.
